Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-06-11 15:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Security), Dana Morris (Sable Head of Security), Raj Patel (Sable Platform Engineer), Lina Gomez (Sable Compliance), Tom Brewer (CTO joined 00:12:30)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through their data residency options, region pinning, and KMS/BYOK integration for a health customer wanting EU-only processing for patient records. Topics:
- Data residency & region pinning
- KMS / BYOK integration and HSM options

- Audit logs and retention/export

- Latency/cost tradeoffs for EU-only routing

Action items (auto): see metadata action_items

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood, we do inference hosting and private deployments, happy to run through the security items you flagged.
[00:15] Dana Morris: Great thanks, we've got a few items on the deck, mostly around ensuring EU patient data never leaves the EU, also key management and audit requirements, um and just high level posture like SOC2 and ISO.
[00:28] Marco Ruiz: Quick intro from my side, I'm Marco, solutions engineer, I'll walk through KMS options and how region pinning works in practice, and Priya will cover subprocessors and SOC/ISO artifacts.
[00:40] Priya Nair: Hi, yes Priya here, I manage product security so I'll cover subprocessor list, log/export guarantees, and encryption details.
[00:51] Raj Patel: Raj here, platform eng, we need a clear path for BYOK, or KMS integration, and we need audit logs shipped to our SIEM in the EU. What are your export hooks?
[01:05] Marco Ruiz: Right, so at a high level we support three deployment modes - hosted API, dedicated, and private. For EU-only processing you have two practical options: host in our EU region with strong region pinning, or run Redwood Private in your VPC. Each has different tradeoffs.
[01:25] Dana Morris: We prefer not to run on-prem for now, so the EU region pinning is our primary ask. But we need guarantees that requests from EU customers are processed and stored in EU datacenters, no cross-border fallback unless it's an explicit, auditable failover.
[01:45] Priya Nair: Understood. Our platform supports region affinity policies; you can configure strict region pinning so requests are routed only to EU-hosted capacity. We also have a configurable fallback policy - by default we do not route cross-border. If you need a fallback, that would be an explicit policy and we can surface it in audit logs and require a customer opt-in.
[02:05] Lina Gomez: Can you show how that's recorded in logs? We need proof for our auditors that no cross-border processing occurred.
[02:14] Marco Ruiz: Sure, log entries include request headers, region of execution, model variant, and the availability zone ID. We can provide a daily export or streaming export of audit logs to your EU LogHub or S3 bucket with SSE and EU-only endpoints. There's a small note: the hosted API metadata sometimes uses shorthand that the transcription might confuse, it's the request routing ID that'll show you which cluster handled the call.
[02:40] Raj Patel: What's retention on those logs? We typically need 7 years for medical telemetry, but at a minimum 1 year for our compliance team.
[02:49] Priya Nair: Audit logs retention is configurable. By default we retain 90 days in our console, but for enterprise customers we can configure longer retention and also provide an export to your storage. We'll include retention SLAs in the pilot contract.
[03:05] Tom Brewer: Joining now, sorry for late jump, CTO here. Big question: BYOK vs Redwood-managed KMS — which is supported in the EU region and how does key escrow/rotations work?
[03:20] Marco Ruiz: We support several patterns: our managed keys (Redwood-managed KMS), customer-managed keys in cloud KMS (e.g., AWS KMS in eu-west-1, Google KMS in europe-west4), and dedicated HSM integration for Private. For hosted EU region we can do BYOK using your cloud KMS keys in the same region; we use envelope encryption so the data keys are generated by Redwood runtime but wrapped by your KMS key. Rotations are orchestrated via key versioning and we can do a key rotation window with rewrap operations.
[03:48] Dana Morris: If we do BYOK with AWS KMS eu-west-1, can Redwood access wrapped keys outside of EU for any reason?
[03:56] Priya Nair: No. If you configure a KMS key in an EU region and strict pinning, the unwrapping happens in the EU cluster that has access to the KMS endpoint. We don't move raw keys out of region; the runtime requests decryption from the cloud KMS endpoint in the region.
[04:15] Raj Patel: Do you support multi-KMS for failover? If a region goes down, we need a documented emergency procedure.
[04:23] Marco Ruiz: We can set multi-KMS configs but that's effectively a cross-region failover and would invoke cross-border processing if the failover is to a non-EU KMS. We treat that as an explicit opt-in workflow and it will appear in the audit trail. For health workloads we usually recommend reserved capacity in the EU region or Private deployment to avoid failovers.
[04:45] Dana Morris: Let's talk subprocessors. We have strict vendor policies, we need to know which subprocessors have access to the data and where they're located.
[04:54] Priya Nair: We'll share the current subprocessor inventory. Today it includes cloud infra providers (AWS eu-west-1, GCP europe-west4), a caching CDN in the EU region, and a small set of monitoring vendors — we can provide contractual EU-only subprocessors for sensitive data. Note that certain low-level telemetry (infra logs) may be processed by cloud providers in their control plane, we'll call that out in the subprocessor list.
[05:22] Lina Gomez: And what about third-party model providers or benchmarking partners — do they ever see data?
[05:28] Avery Chen: Good callout. Our model catalog is curated; for hosted customers, we generally serve models from our vetted catalog. If you opt into specialized models or external scoring services, we will flag those as subprocessors and require your explicit approval — they would be listed and contractually limited.
[05:44] Dana Morris: SOC2/ISO, can you provide those artifacts? Our procurement needs Type II and ISO27001 certification evidence.
[05:52] Priya Nair: Absolutely. We'll attach SOC2 Type II report (redacted) and our ISO27001 certificate. We also have a security whitepaper that explains network segmentation, key handling, and audit controls.
[06:03] Raj Patel: On SSO and RBAC, we use SAML SSO with SCIM provision for groups. Need role separation so only certain users can initiate BYOK or change region policy. How granular is your RBAC?
[06:18] Marco Ruiz: We support SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning, and RBAC with role-level permissions down to route/model-level operations. We also support token-level auditing. For BYOK and region policy changes we restrict those to admin roles and require 2-person approval in the console; we can integrate with your SSO provider to map groups to those roles.
[06:40] Tom Brewer: Do you provide separation between billing/admin and data ops? Our finance team should not be able to view raw request logs.
[06:48] Priya Nair: Yes, we have distinct roles and scopes; billing and usage views are separate from audit and request content. Request content is never exposed in the billing UI. We'll show the role matrix in the next deck.
[07:05] Dana Morris: A couple more technicals: encryption at rest, in transit, and ephemeral in-memory protections for KV cache — since inference loads model weights and cache, we need assurances KV cache isn't spillable.
[07:20] Marco Ruiz: In-transit TLS is mandatory. At-rest uses envelope encryption with customer-managed KMS as discussed. KV cache is memory-resident in the serving nodes and we use kernel memory protections; for dedicated/private deployments you can request encrypted swap and stricter host-level controls. We can provide a short security appendix on memory protections.
[07:44] Raj Patel: If we do a pilot, we'd like logging exported to our SIEM in eu-west-1, KMS in eu-west-1, and the runtime pinned to EU clusters. How do you validate no cross-border traffic at scale?
[08:00] Priya Nair: We'll run a network capture exercise during the pilot and provide an execution provenance report — timestamps, cluster IDs, and proof of KMS region endpoints used. We'll also provide automated daily attestations during the pilot window.
[08:20] Dana Morris: Cost and latency impact? If everything is EU-local only, do we see a cost premium?
[08:27] Marco Ruiz: Slight cost delta depending on capacity footprint and reserved instances in EU. Latency for EU customers will generally improve if traffic stays local; routing to EU-only capacity reduces egress variability. The premium usually comes from reserved capacity pricing and EU region hardware costs. We'll include a cost estimate in the pilot paperwork.
[08:45] Lina Gomez: One compliance scenario: if a lawful request is served by a non-EU authority, what happens? Any cross-border legal exposure?
[08:55] Priya Nair: We provide transparency on subpoenas and governmental requests per our legal obligations. For EU-only configurations, we recommend contractual protections and DPA clauses; we'll surface our transparency report and the process we use for governmental requests.
[09:10] Tom Brewer: Any third-party escrow or forensic access model? For certain regulated customers we've used KMS escrow with a trusted third party.
[09:18] Marco Ruiz: We have options for KMS escrow and for long-term key escrow with an independent escrow provider, that's typically part of an enterprise contract. We'll need to scope that separately.
[09:30] Dana Morris: Good. Can you walk us through a specific example of a request lifecycle and what logs we get?
[09:38] Marco Ruiz: Sure. Example: inbound API call from EU client -> ingress LB in eu-west -> request routed to EU serving cluster based on policy -> runtime allocates KV cache, retrieves data key, calls your KMS in eu-west-1 to unwrap the data key -> generation happens locally -> response streaming back. Logs emitted: ingress IP + geo, routing ID, cluster ID, KMS call id, model ID, token counts, and operation result. Those logs can be exported to your ingestion endpoint.
[10:12] Raj Patel: About KV cache — does it ever get checkpointed to disk?
[10:18] Marco Ruiz: Not for ephemeral caches. We avoid checkpointing KV cache to disk in hosted EU clusters for privacy workloads. For model state we only persist checkpoints to encrypted object stores when explicitly requested, with customer approval.
[10:35] Dana Morris: Ok we need that documented in the pilot scope.
[10:40] Marco Ruiz: Noted.
[10:43] Avery Chen: Quick logistics, we'll share the SOC2/ISO, subprocessor list, and pilot SOW. Can we agree on a pilot window?
[10:52] Raj Patel: We prefer a two-week pilot starting around June 29, pending legal review.
[10:59] Avery Chen: That works on our side — Marco can run the BYOK walkthrough during the pilot start.
[11:06] Marco Ruiz: I'll prepare a test matrix: BYOK integration, log export, region pinning validation, KMS failover scenario (opt-in), and latency benchmarking.
[11:18] Dana Morris: One more question about model outputs — do you keep any long-term artifacts from inference results in logs or store outputs? Our policy forbids storing patient PII even in debug logs.
[11:30] Priya Nair: We don't store raw model outputs in audit logs. Logs contain metadata only. If you need posture for debugging we can do redacted traces or on-demand dumps under your control.
[11:45] Lina Gomez: What about encryption keys for dev/test clusters — do they ever use the same KMS as prod?
[11:52] Marco Ruiz: By default dev/test uses separate keys; we can segregate and emulate prod in the pilot if you'd like.
[12:00] Tom Brewer: Any blockers for us to start the pilot from your side?
[12:06] Avery Chen: No blockers, we just need signed NDA and the pilot SOW. We'll include the compliance pack.
[12:14] Raj Patel: We'll try to get the NDA back next week.
[12:20] Dana Morris: OK good.
[12:24] (cross-talk)
[25:00] Marco Ruiz: I've pasted a diagram in the chat showing region pinning and KMS flows, if folks can't see I'll re-share after the call.
[33:10] Dana Morris: A note on subprocessors: can we get a redline of the DPA to show EU-only subprocessors clause?
[33:20] Priya Nair: Yes we can propose language, and our legal team is used to adding region-bound subprocessors clauses for healthcare customers.
[40:30] Raj Patel: For the BYOK test we want to simulate a KMS outage to see the behavior — but we don't want any data to cross-border during that test. Can you run a controlled failover that stays in-region and just shows behavior?
[40:45] Marco Ruiz: We can simulate a KMS unavailability and prove no cross-border unwrapping happened. For a full cross-region failover, that's opt-in only.
[48:00] Tom Brewer: I'm comfortable with the next steps. If your security artifacts check out, procurement will push for a pilot.
[48:10] Avery Chen: Great. Quick recap of next steps: we send artifacts (SOC2/ISO), share subprocessor map, Marco sends BYOK runbook and test matrix, Raj shares sample PII flow, schedule pilot start week of 2026-06-29.
[48:35] Dana Morris: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[48:38] Marco Ruiz: Thanks, ending early for some folks but we'll follow up in email.
